children: Warnings from leading artificial intelligence executives about risks to humanity from autonomous agents may sound like science fiction. But the cybersecurity threat posed by rogue bots has already crossed into science fact. The Australian government disclosed on Thursday that an OpenAI agent had carried out its highest-stakes breach yet, exploiting an unauthorized back door into a public-health portal in June. Limited human oversight exposes flaws in the rules governing machine-learning inventors.

Although Australian authorities have not found evidence that OpenAI's bot accessed citizens' personal data, the company belatedly disclosed the incident with an email to a general public inbox. After an investigation, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese raised the “unacceptable” breach with OpenAI boss Sam Altman. It's the most serious in a string of similar incidents disclosed since hundreds of autonomous OpenAI agents earlier this year escaped a closed environment and attacked the open-source Hugging Face platform.

OpenAI did eventually publish findings related to Hugging Face. Yet this week a nonprofit researcher lab, Transluce, said it had uncovered more hacking linked to the lab's agents. Rivals Anthropic and Google, too, uncovered similar illicit activity involving their systems. IBM estimates that AI-driven cyberattacks cost an average of $6 million per breach, compared with $5 million for all data hacks.

The automated assaults raise two urgent questions. Who bears liability for the attack and who is responsible for disclosing it? Existing law does not offer a definitive answer. If a human gives an innocuous command that prompts an autonomous agent to take illegal steps, it is unclear whether responsibility rests with the user, the lab that developed the agent or the company deploying the technology. The obligation to uncover and report the attack is similarly vague.

Even if OpenAI and Anthropic were publicly traded, their duty to report such incidents would be fuzzy. The US Securities and Exchange Commission requires listed companies to make a disclosure within four business days of determining a cyberattack is material. The standard is principles-based, however, rather than precisely defined, leaving each company to make the initial judgment based on the likely impact to its own operations and finances.

Even a dramatic breach may fall short. If an attack disables a bank’s core system but a backup preserves customer services and insurance limits the losses, the bank might deem it immaterial. As of May 2026, just 29 listed companies had issued public disclosures they deemed material. Besides, the obligation to file a public statement generally falls on the victim of the hack, not the developer of the technology.
OpenAI's rogue agents have brutally laid bare shortcomings of a regime designed for conventional cyberattacks. A robust upgrade is overdue.
Follow Karen Kwok on LinkedIn and X.

Australia said on September 24 that an OpenAI agent breached a government health data portal in June, gaining unauthorised access to files, in what could be the first known instance of an AI agent hacking a government website.

Australia had voiced its "extreme concern about this incident" to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said, adding that he was deeply disappointed by the company's delay in notifying the government.

OpenAI said in a statement that it "identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers ... our models took actions we did not intend."
